nutshell: When using an off-the-shelf Re-ID system to estimate how many distinct individuals appear in a large image collection, simple clustering (k-means + elbow heuristic) can be off by a factor of two or more because the underlying pairwise similarity is imperfect. This paper reframes population-size estimation as estimating the number of connected components in an unknown similarity graph, and proposes Nested Importance Sampling (Nested-IS): a human-in-the-loop estimator that queries a tiny, cleverly-biased sample of 'same/different' pairs to produce an asymptotically unbiased count with confidence intervals, without needing to solve the full clustering problem.
contributions: Key reduction (Lemma 1): the true number of clusters K in a similarity graph equals the sum over all vertices of 1/(1+degree(u)) - this turns population counting into estimating an expectation, which can be approximated by sampling rather than requiring full graph construction or clustering.

Nested Importance Sampling estimator: a two-stage sampling scheme that samples vertices biased toward low estimated degree (isolated individuals, who contribute most to the count) via Q(u), then samples each vertex's likely neighbors biased toward high approximate similarity via q_u(v) - using the imperfect off-the-shelf similarity only as an importance-sampling proposal, while human 'same/not' labels on the sampled pairs correct the estimate to remain asymptotically unbiased (Theorem 1) even though the proposal itself is wrong.
Closed-form 95% confidence intervals derived from the estimator's asymptotic normality, giving a principled stopping rule for how much human vetting effort is enough - not just a point estimate.

A strong farthest-first-traversal (FFT) baseline that directly targets population-count estimation (rather than adapting general active-clustering methods) and already beats prior active clustering approaches, though without statistical guarantees.

Validated across 7 real animal Re-ID datasets (varying scale, class imbalance, and embedding accuracy) using MegaDescriptor embeddings, reducing typical count error from ~80% (k-means) or ~69% (connected components) down to an average 12.3% while vetting a small fraction of all possible pairs.
deficiencies: The abstract's headline claim ('vetting a fraction, often less than 0.002%, of total pairs') is only representative of the 5 easier datasets - on the two hardest and most realistic ones (WhaleSharkID, GiraffeZebraID: large, long-tailed, ~62% base Re-ID accuracy), NIS needs 0.16% of all pairs to reach single-digit error, two orders of magnitude more effort than the headline number suggests for exactly the deployment conditions closest to real-world use.

The confidence-interval coverage analysis (Fig. 6) shows actual coverage is well below the nominal 95% at low sample sizes, only approaching 95% after roughly 0.02-0.04% of pairs are sampled - meaning the 'stop once the CI is tight enough' guidance is least reliable in exactly the low-budget regime where a user most needs to trust it to decide whether to keep vetting.

The estimator's bias is proven only O(1/M) and vanishes asymptotically (Theorem 1); the paper's own empirical bias plot (Fig. 6-right) confirms a real negative bias at low sample counts that shrinks 'rapidly' but not immediately, so early low-budget estimates - the paper's main selling point - can systematically undercount before that convergence kicks in.

The clustering-accuracy comparison (Fig. 8, Sec. 5) claiming that spending human effort to estimate k (then running k-means) beats spending the same effort on active clustering (pck-means+AL) directly is shown at what the text only describes as 'similar' human effort for one setting per dataset - there's no reported query-count parity check or effort-sensitivity sweep confirming the conclusion holds robustly across different effort budgets rather than the specific point shown.
notable: The core idea - estimate 'how many distinct groups exist' by biased sampling of rare/isolated items and their likely neighbors, without ever building the full similarity graph or solving clustering - is a genuinely reusable pattern beyond animal Re-ID: it applies to any task needing a group-count estimate under a noisy pairwise similarity, e.g. deduplication, entity resolution, or novel-category discovery in other modalities. Also worth flagging: the finding that human budget is better spent estimating k first (then running plain k-means) than on directly guiding active clustering (Fig. 8) is a mildly counter-intuitive result for the active-clustering community, presented almost in passing despite being one of the paper's more practically actionable takeaways.
